articles.title: 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure
articles.summary: Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust…

image.caption: A mural at the Bonn exhibition shows people moments before being sent to the gas chambersImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

blocks.caption: Jens-Christian Wagner reports on rampant disrespect at the Buchenwald Memorial and warns against the distortion of historyImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner says that Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.
The new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.
Moralizing doesn't help people learn

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner says. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students. "Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit."

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explains. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

blocks.caption: Visiting a Holocaust memorial site is a required part of the curriculum at many schoolsImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner says, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example. "For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism."
Holocaust survivor: 'The number tattooed on my arm was always there'
Eva Umlauf knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition. Now, she's 83.

But in November 1944, she was just two years old when the Nazis deported her, her pregnant mother and her father from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using them as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.
Germany's darkest chapter: Auschwitz and the Holocaust

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Eva's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her. Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

blocks.caption: Eva Umlauf has been president of the International Auschwitz Committee since 2025Image: Alessandra Schellnegger/SZ Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eva Umlauf: 'I cannot forgive'
Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and Eva moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she says. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

blocks.caption: An interactive digital testimony has been created for the exhibition, for which Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf answered 1,000 questionsImage: Bright White Ltd.

blocks.text: It was not until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."
'Take care of your country'

Eva Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stresses. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. (…) You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color." She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."
The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Poland begins two days of mourning over Krakow shooting
articles.summary: Mourners left candles in Krakow's main market square to honor the victims of the attack. Police confirmed that the bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his parents and sister.

image.caption: Mourners lay candles in Krakow's main square to pay their respects Image: Jakub Porzycki/REUTERS

blocks.text: Poland began two days of mourning on Sunday, a day after killed six people and wounded 15 others were shot in Krakow's main market square.
The attack occurred in Main Square (Rynek Glowny) in the Old Town of Poland's second-largest city on Saturday. The area is a popular tourist attraction.
In addition to the six people killed in the square, three bodies found at the suspect's home were the bodies of his sister, mother and father, police said Sunday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labeled the attack an act of far-right "terrorism," but authorities have not given a possible motive.
Mourners left candles in the square to pay tribute to the victims of the shooting. Black flags and Polish flags with black ribbons were also seen in the city.
The square remained partially sealed off on Sunday morning as authorities continued investigations.

blocks.caption: The site of the shooting remained partially cordoned off on Sunday morningImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: What do we know about the shooting in Krakow's Main Square?
The 24-year-old suspect, who was wearing military fatigues at the time of the attack, allegedly shot at people at random as he drove around the square.
He was wounded by police and is in critical condition in hospital.
Polish authorities say the man held right-wing extremist and ultranationalist views.
"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said at a news conference.
A British national was among the dead, and among the wounded were citizens of Austria, the United Kingdom, Germany, Portugal and Russia, according to authorities.
Two police officers were wounded while confronting the suspect and are in hospital. Officials have launched an appeal for blood donations for one of the officers, who is in critical condition.
The Krakow Carriage Driver's Association told Polish news agency PAP that several horse-drawn carriage drivers were seriously injured in the shooting.
Police confirm three bodies found were members of suspect's family
Police said on Sunday that three bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his sister, mother and father.
The family home is in the town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.
Police said that several firearms were seized from the apartment.
The suspect had no previous criminal record, according to Polish media reports.
He and his father were members of a shooting club.

articles.title: How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
articles.summary: Video authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment gunshots rang out in Krakow's main market square.

blocks.text: Six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second largest city, on Saturday.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows about a dozen people running inside two buildings before a black car with its front window open passes, followed by a police car.
Another video shows the moment that gunshots were heard in the city's main market square.
Poland's interior minister described the suspect - a 25-year-old Polish citizen - as being inspired by "far-right ideologies"; police said he used "military weapons" in the attack.
Hours after the attack, Polish PM Donald Tusk said three other bodies were found at the suspect's home, which is still being searched.

articles.title: Analysis of crime-scene blood and bullets can be pivotal in court cases. But how reliable is it?
articles.summary: Ballistic and blood spatter analysis are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, according to…

image.caption: A Texas Ranger holds a shell casing discovered at the crime scene as he testifies in a murder trial in Stephenville, Texas, in February 2015. A new analysis points to 'significant methodological flaws' in the research that backs up ballistics as a discipline. (Tom Fox/Pool/The Dallas Morning News/Th

blocks.text: World

Ballistic and blood spatter analysis are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, according to new research — while lawyers and judges don’t challenge those conclusions enough.
Researcher questions extent of what forensic evidence reveals, says lawyers need to challenge experts in court

Forensic analysis has a reputation for being reliably accurate, an assumption that's been polished by many crime TV dramas where ballistics and blood-spatter teams uncover essential evidence to catch the perpetrator.
But that assumption has found its way into courtrooms, where the accuracy of forensic analysis is rarely questioned, according to new research.

Both ballistic and blood spatter analysis, which examine evidence from a crime scene, are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, says researcher Sara Gordon — while lawyers and judges don’t challenge those conclusions enough.

"They're admitted largely because they've always been admitted and people just sort of assume that they're reliable," says Gordon, an associate professor at Peter A. Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia.

items: How Toronto police gather clues from guns seized off city streets

blocks.text: Qualified and admissible expert testimony on forensic evidence can provide "significant assistance" in understanding specific information in a case, a fact sheet from the Department of Justice says. Canada’s courts have allowed it to be included in cases for decades.
Using Canadian cases, Gordon examined these forensic and investigative techniques that informed evidence regularly admitted in court.

Her analysis of firearms evidence points to "significant methodological flaws" in the research that backs up ballistics as a discipline that may "underestimate error rates." She concludes that experts often don’t give courts the full story and give "a false impression" of the accuracy of their speciality.
Evidence markers are placed beside shell casings on the street outside a cafe that was shot at in Surrey, B.C., in August 2025. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)
Bullet proof?

To connect a bullet or casing found at a crime scene to a caliber of gun, ballistics examiners will compare other bullets or casings shot from test guns and examine them under a microscope to look for similarities.
Eventually a forensic scientist may end up in a courtroom testifying that the evidence found at a crime scene is or isn’t a match, citing research from their field to back up their conclusions.

Gordon says examiners will often testify that the error rate of the ballistics field is somewhere between one and two per cent. But the studies she examined for her research reported an error rate as high as 50 per cent.
She also says there are no set standards for the minimum number of similarities needed to match bullets.
"It's largely a subjective analysis," she said.
Courts must start questioning reliability of some forensic evidence, researcher says

Her research, which follows similar audits of forensic evidence in the United States, cites a case in Ontario in 2021, where a firearms examiner conceded under cross-examination that her conclusion — that shell casings from a crime scene matched a handgun found in the accused's apartment — was subjective.

The examiner later added there was “no specific number of agreements required between two items for her to conclude that there was a match" and she formed her opinion because she believed a match was "within the limits of practical certainty."

items: A$AP Rocky's trial starts with clash over ballistics report

blocks.text: The issue came to a head in a Chicago courtroom in 2023, where a judge, moved by a lack of "objective forensic based reasons," banned the use of ballistics matching in a criminal case.

The judge then reviewed a dozen other cases that resulted in a wrongful conviction from flawed ballistics matching, labelling it a "wake-up call to courts operating as rubber stamps in blindly finding general acceptance" of this type of evidence.

Bullet fragments are displayed on a screen in a Utah courtroom on July 9, during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk. (Spenser Heaps/Pool/The Associated Press)
Drawing from such decisions, Gordon argues that some ballistic experts shouldn't be testifying in cases where the science doesn't give them the ability to draw conclusions.
One senior forensic scientist who regularly testifies in court says being transparent about a discipline's limitations is key.

Darryl Barr, who examines weapons and tools linked to crimes for Bulletproof Forensic Consulting, maintains there is "a scientific basis for firearms examinations" and plenty of empirical evidence that supports experts' determinations — but he concedes they could do better at making that clearer in court.
Barr says he's reassured by the fact that virtually every country in the world uses forensic analysis as part of its judicial process, and adds that any scrutiny of his discipline is welcomed.
"Science improves through scrutiny and forensic science is not any different, obviously," he said.

Investigators gather ballistic evidence at two separate crime scenes. Left, New York police photograph bullets on the sidewalk where Brian Thompson, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, was fatally shot on Dec. 4, 2024. Right, the copper jacket of a bullet found near the scene of a shooting close to the White House on May 24 this year. (AP Photo/Stefan Jeremiah / AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
The CSI effect
Part of a prosecution or defence counsel's role is to scrutinize each other’s evidence. But digging into the accuracy of the science of forensic evidence doesn’t happen often, says Gordon.

She thinks part of the reason is that society at large has come to think ballistics and blood spatter are as definitive as DNA evidence and can reveal crucial details in an investigation — in part due to crime shows like Law and Order and the many spin-offs of CSI.
For example — despite what a slick, sunglasses-wearing fictional detective might say — the science of blood spatter cannot indicate if a person was acting deliberately or not.
A physical comparison supervisor at the Vermont Forensic Laboratory examines a shell casing in March 2015. (Wilson Ring/The Associated Press)
Gordon's separate research on blood spatter analysis found the detail to which some experts testify is sometimes very specific, such as inferring what an accused's mental state might have been.

She points to a B.C. case from 2009 where the Crown used analysis of blood patterns in a crime scene to reconstruct the actions of the accused, arguing he had guilty intent because of the way blood was "projected" during the attack.

items: Investigators found presumed blood stains in garage years after alleged murder, court hears

blocks.text: "There are no studies testing or establishing an error rate for conclusions about an individual’s mental state based on bloodstain patterns," she writes in her research.
"There's just no indication, in the science, that we can make those sorts of conclusions," she told CBC News.
'Frailties of the evidence'
The danger of lawyers not challenging expert witness testimony in court is recognized in case law, says Rebecca McConchie, president of the Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia.
So, too, is the risk of judges and juries not appreciating the "frailties of the evidence when assessing it," she said in a statement to CBC News.
"It is so important for people to keep an open mind when they hear about criminal justice issues or evidence held out as obvious proof of a person’s guilt," McConchie said.
A statue of Themis, goddess of justice, at the B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver, pictured on Oct. 6. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
Ultimately, Gordon says, Canada has received far less attention in legal literature and she wants her studies to make the country's courts better at doing their job of determining guilt or innocence.

She says her work is about providing information about the evidence behind the evidence for lawyers and judges to be able to ask more questions — to "lay that out for them in a way that just makes them view the evidence a little bit more skeptically."

items: Jury hears forensic expert detail evidence in 30-year cold case sex assault trial

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the RCMP, which provides forensic services across Canada, said it was aware of the research and that it's still committed to using established scientific methodologies, quality assurance processes and professional standards in its work.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Georgie Smyth is a CBC Network Reporter and Producer in Vancouver. She's worked for BBC World News in London and for Nine News in Australia. She's focused on local, national and international stories that affect all Canadians. Got an idea or story tip? Email: georgina.smyth@cbc.ca

articles.title: Pope’s visit to Argentina sets up showdown with ‘hyper-capitalist’ Milei
articles.summary:
President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’

Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are…

blocks.text: Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.

But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.

“[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”.

Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy.

The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024.

Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.”
Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.”

But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation.

Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.”

Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.”

Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse.

The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”.

All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself.

“I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel.

Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.”

Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.”
To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.”

That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”.

But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.

Nevertheless, a majority of Argentines expect a “message from the pope focused on the social and humanitarian agenda”. Grabois notes the transformative impact that first Francis and now Leo have had “with left-leaning activists” in Argentina. “I’m not speaking about atheists, but outright anticlerical people. People who, 10 years ago, held views that were very, very hostile toward the church,” he said. “I even see them as more fervent [about the visit] than typical churchgoers who attend Sunday Mass.” For Grabois, “in the face of dehumanisation, ordinary people are taking refuge in the only global voice that’s speaking out about this today – which is Francis and Leo’s.”

articles.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
articles.summary: With fears of cyberattacks, conflict and major disruption to daily life grow in Europe, governments are urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. But in Britain, the culture of stockpiling supplies…

image.caption: A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting Intermarché and Cooperative U chains. Britain is among many European government introducing emergency preparedness campaigns. (Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The last time any British government launched a national public preparedness campaign was at the peak of the Cold War in 1980.

The “Protect and Survive” message was delivered in short, eerie-looking public information broadcasts and booklets, meant to advise people on how to prepare for a nuclear attack. The campaign — whose guidance included hiding under a heavy table or tips about how to store a dead body in the house for five days — backfired and was ridiculed. Brits realized little would protect them from a thermonuclear strike, leaving them feeling that preparation was pointless as survival would be futile.

Nearly 50 years on, the head of the British Army, Gen. Sir Roland Walker, addressed some 700 soldiers last month at Britain's biggest garrison in northern England. The "business of soldiering" had returned to the national psyche, he told members of the light, high-readiness global response force, adding that anyone following world affairs will realize there is “extreme jeopardy."

“The political leaders of this country,” he said, “will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country about just what is going on, and where the risk lies, and what the nation ... must need to be prepared to do.”

Exactly one week later, Britain’s “Be Ready” campaign was unveiled, a guide on preparing for 72 hours of self-sufficiency in the event of an emergency, be it a climate crisis, cyber disruptions or threats by hostile states.

“It’s something that emergency planners have been wanting for a very long time,” said Lucy Easthope, a global disaster recovery specialist. Easthope has advised in emergencies from the Novichok poisonings in Salisbury, England, to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and 9/11.
Easthope says what the public wants is reassurance — not negative and depressing messaging.
“Ancient DNA, by that I mean 30 years ago, is being reawoken,” she told CBC News. “This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable.
“I’m really pleased in the U.K. we haven’t resorted to fear messaging.”
Other European nations have also recently introduced or updated their emergency guidance, including France, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Germany and Poland.

Ottawa, too, has reiterated its longstanding advice. But unlike Canada with its emergency preparedness week — an annual event since 1996 — Britain faces a cultural hurdle, with the word "preparedness" not even being in most Brits' vocabulary. The U.K. has largely relied on community resilience to short-term disruptions, rather than self sufficiency. Now, it faces the challenge of convincing people that they must be prepared for the worst — without sending them into a panic.
Widespread warnings
In Hertfordshire, north of London, family physician Nyari Matebwe says her first reaction was to roll her eyes and ignore it.
“I feel like it’s scaremonger-y, or the skeptic in me thinks maybe they’re hiding something from us … another distraction from the real issues,” she said.

The recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers in multiple European countries and attempts to raise temperatures in French medical fridges containing critical blood donation stocks have made her question her own skepticism.
“After the recent airplane bomb hoaxes, I did start to think about it a bit more,” said Matebwe, whose teenage daughter is pushing her to take the prepping message seriously.
Sweden is advising seven days, Germany up to 10, but the U.K., like Canada, has settled on three days' survival off-grid.
Europe's wave of bomb threats spreads from airports to newsrooms
School parents’ WhatsApp groups are lighting up with conversations
“I want to stockpile but I’m in a state of inertia,” one parent wrote. “My husband is totally unbothered.”
Another asked, “How will we cook if there’s no gas or electricity?” while one raised concern about rising crime rates and the risk of keeping cash at home.
Warnings have been widespread recently.

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the government’s signals agency GCHQ and the Five Eyes intelligence sharing group that includes Canada, told CBC News: “This is a moment of urgency.”

items: Russia continues its attacks on power facilities in Kyiv as temperatures drop ahead of winter
The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?

blocks.text: The NCSC says AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the power stations, airports and hospitals in the U.K. within two years.
In Horne’s annual state of the cyber nation address, he said “military networks are subjected to sustained and persistent, widespread attempts to penetrate our systems."
That included Russian hybrid warfare campaigns, he said.
“All countries need to be taking this moment seriously," he told CBC News. “There are loads of vulnerabilities that do not need to be there,” which he said the country's adversaries are exploiting.
'Hard times have been forgotten'
Outside the need for companies to keep their technology safe, Horne said at home it is a case of keeping devices up to date and using passkeys.
“You do need to be thinking about, 'do I need to be having the levels of connectivity of devices across my house, apartment' … not unnecessarily introducing potential vulnerabilities.”
There are some who see the “Be Ready” messaging as another example of the "nanny state," or the government telling them how to live.
Others think cultural attitudes play a part.
Getting prepped to deal with emergencies
Luis Martinez Arnal, an IT professional from Spain now based in London, says his Mexican wife automatically prepares for emergencies, having grown up in a country prone to earthquakes.
“But in the U.K.,” Arnal said, “hard times have been forgotten.”
The accessibility of everything, he added, “psychologically is making us feel more comfortable.”

The recent cyberattacks have created a heightened sense of anxiety across Europe, and as people grow more reliant on the internet, questions are being asked how anyone can prepare to stay connected if it went down. Those haven't been easily answered — especially as Britain has long planned to switch all copper-wire landline phones to internet use-only from the end of January 2027.
“Call me crazy, but following the new guidelines, I do feel a bit nervous,” said one London mother, Amee Doshi, pointing to talk about the potential for a world war.

A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is seen stopped at a police roadblock on Sept. 27, in Fairford, U.K. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about 1.6 kilometres from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)
Others appear to be taking to it like true preppers.
“We bulk-buy,” said Preyal Shah, a working mother from Harrow in northwest London.
“I even now have 10 kilograms of rice, five kilograms of pasta … multiple cases of tinned food, each type being 12 tins.”
Preyal said she is also stockpiling newspapers to light a coal-burning stove: “Back to basics.”
Competing crises
In October, British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that the country needs to be “ready for war in 1,000 days," flagging the potential of Russian aggression.
“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” he said.
“We’ve just got so many competing crises at the moment … and war in Europe,” said Reena Patel, a lawyer from north London, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking war is coming but…” she said, listing off all she wants to buy, from a wind-up radio to water purification filters.
“The only thing I have in my control is to try to be a little bit prepared.”

articles.title: My son is surrounded by English. But Korean won't reach him without me
articles.summary: As a Korean mother living in Canada, Noeul Kang finds herself constantly thinking about what it means to give her son a language that isn't regularly spoken outside their home.

image.caption: As a Korean mother living in Canada, Noeul Kang finds herself constantly thinking about what it means to give her son a language that isn't spoken outside their home. (Hyeseon Yang)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
As a Korean mother living in Canada, Noeul Kang finds herself constantly thinking about what it means to give her son a language that isn't regularly spoken outside their home.
I feel unexpected pressure knowing that I am my son’s primary connection to his heritage
This First Person is the experience of Noeul Kang, who lives in Ottawa. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

I was born and raised in South Korea. In 2018, I immigrated to Canada in my late 20s. I speak English and can get through my days without much trouble. But English is not the language in which I feel most like myself.
That language is Korean.
It is the language I turn to when I am emotional, joking, angry or trying to explain something complicated. It is the language in which I know how to express what is closest to my heart.

That's why I speak Korean to my 18-month-old son. From the day he was born, I have spoken to him in Korean. I tell him to come to mommy, eat his food, put on his shoes or look at the dog outside, even when I am not sure how much Korean he understands.
This should be simple. But sometimes, it isn't.

We live in Ottawa, where he will grow up hearing mostly English, along with French. Around English-speaking friends, neighbours and extended family, I sometimes speak English to him, too. Then, when it is just the two of us again, I switch back to Korean. Sometimes, I don't even notice that I have started mixing the two languages.

My husband is white and was born and raised in Canada. He is fluent in Korean, having lived in South Korea for three years, where he worked as an English teacher in a public school. Given that Korean is my mother tongue, we agreed I would take the lead in speaking it to our son. My husband often notices when I mix the two languages, pointing it out: “Korean and English,” as a gentle reminder of our pact.
Every time he does, a small flicker of doubt crosses my mind. Am I doing this right?

items: What no one told me about the land that would become my home

blocks.text: I often feel lonely. There are several Korean communities in Ottawa organized around faith or libraries, but not many Korean playgroups. I spend most of my time with my son at English-speaking and bilingual playgroups. I don't want him to experience only Korean communities. I want him to grow up among people from diverse backgrounds. I simply wish we had more opportunities to connect with other Korean-speaking families, even if only a few times a year.

Recently, I started teaching students from junior kindergarten through high school at a Korean community school on Saturdays. There was a time when I wanted so badly to assimilate into Canadian culture that I avoided jobs related to Korean language and culture. But since giving birth to my son, I have come to understand the importance of knowing your roots and preserving your mother tongue not just to communicate with others, but to understand yourself.
Isn't life, after all, about knowing who you are?
Some of the Korean language books Kang teaches with at the with Ottawa Korean Community School. (Noeul Kang)

And yet, I am not always confident in my choices. Speaking Korean to my son requires a surprising amount of intention. When everyone around us is speaking English, I sometimes hesitate for a split second. Should I just speak English? Would that be easier for him? What if I am making things harder than they need to be?
And yet I choose Korean. Again and again.
It is such a small decision.
“Dog, woof woof” becomes gae meong-meong (개 멍멍).
“Hello” becomes annyeong (안녕).
“Car, vroom vroom” becomes cha bureung-bureung (차 부릉부릉).
“Duck, quack quack” becomes ori gwaek-gwaek (오리 꽥꽥).
I make these choices dozens, perhaps hundreds, of times a day. Each one takes a little energy.
English will come to him anyway. He will hear it at school and speak it with his friends. English will be everywhere. I don't have to fight for English. But I worry that I have to fight for Korean.
Perhaps that is why I feel so much pressure to get it right.

items: Getting my Canadian permanent residency should have felt like a win. But I've lost a lot along the way

blocks.text: Then, one day, my son said, “Appa.”
Daddy. In Korean. His first Korean word was for his father, not me. I was right there, and somehow, I found it both ironic and wonderful.
Kang often describes the world she and her son see on their walks in Korean. A red maple leaf, for example, is a ppalgan danpungip (빨간 단풍잎). (Hyeseon Yang)
For a moment, that one word felt like proof that all those tiny choices had mattered. That all those times I had spoken Korean, even when I wasn't sure he understood, had led somewhere.

Of course, one word doesn't prove anything. I don't know what his Korean will look like when he starts school. I don't know whether he will always answer me in Korean, or whether one day he will understand everything I say but respond only in English. I don't know whether I will always have the confidence to keep choosing Korean.
Even so, Korean is the language in which I know how to be his mother. So I will keep speaking it, even when I am uncertain.
Because English will find him. But Korean won't reach him without me actively trying.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here’s more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Noeul Kang is a Korean language instructor at the Ottawa Korean Community School. She lives in Ottawa with her husband and son.

articles.title: What needs to happen for Canada to join Europe's flagship student exchange program?
articles.summary: Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe. But how Canada would expand its participation…

image.caption: McGill University in Montreal is seen in 2023. Prime Minister Mark Carney said last month that once Canada becomes a partner country of Erasmus+, 'a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill.' (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe. But how Canada would expand its participation in Erasmus+ is complicated.
EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, but there are details Canada must iron out
Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe.

At last month's Canada-EU summit and in his 2026 budget, Prime Minister Mark Carney reaffirmed the government's interest in expanding Canada's participation in Erasmus+, Europe's internationally recognized student and skills exchange.
"Through this program, a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill," Carney said at the summit in Montreal.
An expert in European integration says the prospect is complex and likely to be expensive — but that it would come with major benefits for Canada's youth and deepening ties with the EU.

items: Carney wants Canada to join Europe's Erasmus+ program. What is it?

blocks.text: Through Erasmus+, students in the EU and select other countries have direct access to funding, institutions and grants that help cover travel and living costs when participating in exchange programs between institutions.
Students are also exempted from the fees for tuition, registration and exams that a Canadian exchange student might typically pay to study in Europe.

But Erasmus+ isn't just an opportunity for students. Its benefits extend to people starting their careers across a wide range of fields, including trainees, apprentices, youth workers and academic staff.
"An apprentice welder in Manitoba could bring or complete their placement with an employer in Italy, bringing new skills home," Carney said.
Many Canadian universities are already partnered with Erasmus+ through independent agreements, but they're limited mostly to exchange opportunities for master's students and faculty members.

Further participation in Erasmus+ could expand funding opportunities for undergraduates as well as youth, training and sport exchanges — all of which are available to EU members and the program's current six associate countries.
How would this work?
Oliver Schmidtke, a University of Victoria professor specializing in European integration, called Canada's proposed involvement in Erasmus+ "a lot of ambition."

"Education is largely a provincial thing in Canada, so how this would land and how the federal government would interact with provincial governments in trying to regulate this … that's a whole range of questions that are open," Schmidtke said.
What could EU associate membership look like for Canada?
And buying into an international exchange program isn't exactly cheap. The United Kingdom is rejoining in January and will pay over $1 billion for its first year.

Canadian universities would have to "pay substantial amounts to be eligible for the full array of services" and provide housing supports and staff to accommodate the Erasmus+ students coming to Canada, Schmidtke said.
The provinces and European Union would also have to iron out credit transfers for participating students — no simple feat.
All current Erasmus+ members and associated third countries follow the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS), simplifying the academic credit transfer process.
When the United Kingdom rejoins, it will be using its own system, but has set up a national framework for how credits will be transferred.
In Canada, even credit transfers between institutions within the same province aren't consistent.

items: Students across Ontario walk out to protest OSAP changes, tuition hike
Ontario estimated to lose more than a 3rd of its international students: StatsCan

blocks.text: This work would come at time of "a lot of financial stress at Canadian universities," Schmidtke said.
He said some of that comes from a reduced number of international students in Canada in recent years — who generally pay higher tuition rates directly to the institutions.

Carney has indicated that the expected costs of joining Erasmus+ won't stop Canada from pursuing that goal. Joining was one of the most concrete examples Carney gave when he announced in September that Canada was pursuing an "alliance for the future" with the EU.
"We don't view this as paying for something," Carney said in Montreal about the overall costs of closer EU integration. "We view this as coming together."

items: Why none of the EU's existing partnerships are the right fit for Canada

blocks.text: Despite these potential complications, Schmidtke believes integration with Erasmus+ will be an "invaluable opportunity" for Canadian students.

"Canada is a bit behind the curve when it comes to internationalizing student experiences, mobility and so forth," Schmidtke said. "So the Erasmus+ program could be a great incentive to expand the international experience of many Canadian students."
Some Canadian universities already involved

The University of Victoria, University of Waterloo, McMaster University, Simon Fraser University, University of Toronto, University of British Columbia and the University of Calgary told CBC News they would be open to exploring participation — or further participation, as some already partner with Erasmus+ — as more details become available.

Western University president Alan Shepard said international engagement is a key part of the student experience at Western, and the university was excited about the opportunities Erasmus+ could create.
"We encourage our students to see themselves as global citizens through opportunities to study, conduct research and gain hands-on experience around the world," Shepard said.
How Canadian students could benefit from EU 'associate member' status

In late October, Université Laval rector Sophie D'Amours and Sorbonne University president Nathalie Drach-Temam penned an open letter in La Presse encouraging the government to integrate Canadian universities into the program.

"The Sorbonne is the oldest French-language university in Europe. Université Laval is the oldest French-language university in the Americas. Our traditions are strong, as is our capacity to help address the challenges of tomorrow," the letter said.
By joining forces, we will be even better placed to promote the common good that universities represent for society."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sophia Laporte is an intern with CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa and a fourth-year journalism and humanities student at Carleton University.

articles.title: India: Delhi chokes on most polluted Diwali eve in 10 years
articles.summary: Delhi was ranked as the world's most polluted major city on the eve of Diwali. Delhi's air pollution is expected to get worse in the coming days. DW has more.

image.caption: Delhi residents woke up Sunday to 'very unhealthy' levels of air pollutionImage: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

blocks.text: November 8, 2026
Delhi most polluted city in world on Diwali eve

blocks.caption: People in the capital woke up to a thick smog as pollution worsened in DelhiImage: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

blocks.text: Delhi awoke Sunday morning enveloped in smog with poor visibility after the previous night saw the worst air quality for Diwali eve in 10 years.
The worst polluted pre-Diwali day was in 2016 when on October 29 the air quality index hit 404 on India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
On Saturday, the day before Diwali, Swiss ​group IQAir had ranked Delhi as the world's most polluted major city.
IQAir said Delhi had a "very unhealthy" air quality index (AQI) of 201 on Sunday.
The air quality is forecast to turn "severe" on Sunday, with Diwali celebrations adding to the pollution.

While vehicular emissions and stubble burning in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana are major contributors to air pollution, Diwali celebrations, which involve large-scale burning of firecrackers, add to the pollution in the city.
The government had already ordered schools in and ​around Delhi to offer online classes, and ​encouraged people to work from home ahead of ⁠the Hindu festival of light.

articles.summary: Senate Committee on Finance Vice Chairperson Senator Risa Hontiveros is expecting Vice President Sara Duterte to attend the Office of the Vice President"s (OVP) budget deliberations, similar to what…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 3:08pm

Senate Committee on Finance Vice Chairperson Senator Risa Hontiveros is expecting Vice President Sara Duterte to attend the Office of the Vice President’s (OVP) budget deliberations similar to what other agency heads do, as a demonstration of proper conduct.

“I expect her to appear. Binanggit ‘yun explicitly ni [Senate President] Sherwin [Gatchalian] nung committee hearing na ineexpect talaga namin na bawat committee hearing hanggang sa plenary nandun ‘yung head of agency at hindi lamang kay VP Duterte lamang sinabi yun,” Hontiveros told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.

(I expect her to appear. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian explicitly mentioned during the committee hearing that we expect every agency head to attend the budget hearings, from the committee level up to the plenary, and this not only applies to the Vice President alone.
"[Kung hindi na naman dumating], I’m sure papansinin namin ‘yan kasi hindi ‘yan proper conduct. Sa kahit sino mang head of agency kahit pa o lalo na Vice President,” she added.
(If she fails to attend again, I’m sure we will take notice because that is not proper conduct for any agency head, especially the Vice President.)
In October, a Senate finance subcommittee panel quickly approved the proposed P785.2 million OVP budget for fiscal year 2027, terminating the briefing after 16 minutes.
Duterte was not present during the budget briefing, but the OVP was represented by its chief of staff, Zuleika Lopez, and other officials.
The OVP said the P785.204 million budget aims to support the agency’s continued delivery of assistance and services to beneficiaries nationwide.
The 2027 budget recommendation includes P220.232 million for Personnel Services (PS), P561.651 million for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.321 million for Capital Outlay.
Meanwhile, P15.544 million is automatically appropriated for the Retirement and Life Insurance Premium (RLIP) of OVP plantilla personnel. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Erwin Tulfo files bill seeking worker protection vs. layoffs due to AI
articles.summary: Senator Erwin Tulfo filed a bill seeking to protect workers from artificial intelligence-driven layoffs by amending the Labor Code to establish clear conditions for terminations and guarantee fair…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 3:01pm

Senator Erwin Tulfo filed a bill seeking to protect workers from artificial intelligence-driven layoffs by amending the Labor Code to establish clear conditions for terminations and guarantee fair compensation.

Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Social Justice, Welfare, and Development, introduced Senate Bill (SB) No. 2563, which proposes key amendments to Article 298 of the Labor Code of the Philippines.

“As companies adopt AI, employees whose jobs become redundant risk losing not only their employment but also their means of supporting their families. Technological progress is inevitable, but Filipino workers should not be left behind or made it bear its costs alone,” Tulfo wrote in his explanatory note.

In a statement on Sunday, the senator said SB No. 2563 requires employers to provide fair separation pay, opportunities for reskilling and redeployment, and advance notice with mandatory consultations for affected workers.
Under the bill, employers can only terminate workers due to AI automation if the following conditions are met:

items: There must be a bona fide introduction of implementation of AI technologies or systems;
AI implementations must be undertaken in good faith;
The purpose for AI introduction or implementation is valid to save cost, enhance efficiency and other justifiable economic reasons;
No other option available for the employer other than to introduce or implement AI technologies and the consequent termination of employee; and
There must be fair and reasonable criteria in selecting employees to be terminated.

blocks.text: Should terminations occur, the bill requires employers to notify the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) at least six months in advance.

It also stipulates that employees terminated under these conditions are entitled to separation pay equal to at least two months pay or to at least two months pay for every year of service, whichever is higher.
Tulfo stressed that before turning to AI automation, employers must first exhaust all efforts to reskill their existing workforce before resorting to layoffs.

“There must be a proactive effort to keep workers away from termination just because AI comes in. We are not only talking about careers here, we are concerned with livelihood and lives of the employees’ families,” the senator said.
Malacañang meanwhile on Friday admitted that AI may displace workers. However, the technology could also bring new opportunities for Filipinos. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Banana producers in Latin America want better pay to cope with effects of climate crisis
articles.summary:
Farmers face big drop in production from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event

Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of…

blocks.text: Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.

High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.

Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.

Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.

Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.

“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.

Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”

Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.
While some businesses, including Sainsbury’s, the Co-op and Waitrose, have taken voluntary steps by sourcing only Faitrade bananas, which guarantee a minimum price, it says there is more work to do.

Eleanor Harrison, the chief executive of Fairtade, said: “The UK’s banana supply depends on the people growing our bananas having the resources they need to adapt to climate change, and to invest in their future. Fair prices, climate resilience and decent work go hand in hand.”
after newsletter promotion
While bananas are becoming harder and more expensive to produce, supermarket prices have remained unchanged for almost 40 years despite rising costs for fertiliser, fuel and labour.

Caoimhe Buckley, the chief corporate affairs officer at the large supplier Fyffes, said: “The long-term sustainability of the banana sector … cannot be separated from purchasing practices. The price of bananas in the supermarket needs to recognise the real and sustainable cost of production, including labour and decent wages, environmental management, human-rights due diligence and the investment necessary to adapt to climate change.”
Research by the Ethical Trading Initiative found that prices paid to suppliers in 2026 did not even cover basic production costs for 66.7% of them.

It said producers need more help to adapt or mitigate climatic changes, which could mean suitable land for banana cultivation could shrink by an average of 61% across Latin America and the Caribbean by 2050, according to research for the Inter-American Development Bank published in 2020.

articles.title: 2027 budget bicam proceedings transcripts to be released, will help track realignments - Lacson
articles.summary: The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027, Senator Panfilo Lacson said…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:55pm

The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 202, Senator Panfilo Lacson said Sunday.
In a statement, Lacson said the transcript would help lawmakers and the public track who pushed for realignment of specific items in the budget.
“Kailangan may minutes ‘yan para maliwanag sino nag-initiate ng amendment at sino nagtulak ng realignment,” Lacson said.
(There should be a transcript containing the minutes so it will be clear who initiated amendments and who pushed for realignments.)
He added that the Senate is also pushing for continued livestreaming of the bicam conference committee discussions.

Aside from continuing transparency measures from the 2026 budget, Lacson said the Senate also plans to identify senators who proposed amendments to the budget bill and posting the proceedings on the Senate’s website.
For the 2027 budget, Lacson said the Senate plans to invite budget advocacy groups like the People’s Budget Coalition to the bicameral proceedings to better ensure transparency.
“Panawagan ko nga vigilance is not enough. Panawagan ko sa kanila baka pwede na sila mag-resort sa shaming para pwedeng tablan ng hiya ang iba,” he said.
(I told the groups that vigilance is not enough and that they should resort to shaming against lawmakers who sneak in questionable realignments.)
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed budget.

Ejercito also confirmed that the bicameral deliberations which would reconcile the Senate and the House of Representatives’ differing versions of the budget bill, would also be livestreamed to allow the public to watch the proceedings in real time.
Lacson also raised concerns over the questionable coordinates in the proposed 2027 national budget flagged by budget advocacy groups.

“Akala ko malayo na ‘yung Leyte, hanggang sa marinig ko yung People’s Budget Coalition, umabot pa ng Celebes Sea. So hindi ito typo error kasi naka-geotag, dapat pinpointed talaga. Yun ang gamit nga ng geotagging, na kung saan madaling hanapin yung project at madaling ma-inspect para pag yung quality control nila, madaling malaman kung talaga nagawa yung proyekto,” the senator said.

(I thought Leyte was already far enough, until the People’s Budget Coalition flagged a project whose coordinates pointed to the Celebes Sea. So this is not a mere typo error because the projects are geotagged and should be pinpointed. That’s what geotagging is for– to make it easy to locate and inspect a project so its quality can be checked and verified.)

Meanwhile, Lacson said senators would relay Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Giovanni Lopez’s requirements for project funding, including program of works, feasibility studies, and geotagging.
The senator also said the Unified Account Code Structure (UACS) throughout the process to ensure smooth tracking of project implementation.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian had said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from the DPWH. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Who are qualified to get DepEd's new laptops for teachers?
articles.summary: The Department of Education released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:31pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.
The DepEd earlier secured over 172,000 units of Apple's MacBook Neo laptops, which the tech giant reportedly acknowledged as its "biggest education deal ever" for its MacBook line.

"Dahil limitado pa ang available units na kayang mabili sa allocated national budget, hindi pa lahat ng guro ay mabibigyan sa round na ito. Sisikapin nating matiyak ang patas at maayos na pamamahagi ng mga laptop," said DepEd.
Who are eligible for the budget MacBook laptops?
DepEd said that it would prioritize schools and teachers who have yet to receive any laptop.
It would also prioritize those personnel holding EdTech leadership roles or those actively helping in teaching with technology.
The beneficiaries should be active employees in the listed school during the selection, it added.
Teachers who still have a working government/school laptop issued last January 2023 to November 6, 2026 are not eligible to receive the brand new units.
However, DepEd said that those who bought their own laptops are not disqualified from receiving MacBook Neo units.

Further, the department said that former laptop recipients can still receive the MacBook Neo units by providing official records declaring that their laptops are unserviceable and decommissioned; lost or damaged because of calamity; or lost due to theft or robbery.
The department said that eligible teachers should have an active DepEd email account and the two-factor authentication must be on.
How will the recipients be chosen?
According to DepEd, there will be a draw if the allotted units are not enough for the priority groups.

Moreover, DepEd reminded that the brand new laptops are government properties. Hence, they cannot be sold or transferred to new owners without the proper authorization by the school head and property custodian.
If a teacher will be transferred to another school, the department said the laptop accountability shall be transferred as well to the new school.
Once a teacher decides to retire or resign, the laptop shall be returned to the supply officer or property custodian.
Each MacBook Neo unit was procured at P43,000, which is P6,900 below the current suggested retail price in the Philippines for the base model.
The DepEd said this included a five-year warranty, which is a first for the agency's laptop procurement, instead of the typical one-year warranty. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News
